STA 112: Lab 01

Qingyang Liu

2026-08-23

Introduction

In this lab, you will practice several fundamental skills for working with data in R. You will learn how to:

  • import an Excel dataset into R;
  • inspect and summarize a dataset;
  • identify and remove missing values;
  • filter observations;
  • calculate summary statistics;
  • create boxplots, histograms, bar charts, and scatterplots; and
  • interpret graphical output.

Please complete each exercise in order. Keep all R code and the associated output in your submitted R Markdown document.

Penguin Data

Before starting the lab, download penguins.xlsx from Canvas and place the file in your R project working directory.

The dataset contains physical measurements and demographic information for 344 penguins observed in the Palmer Archipelago, Antarctica.

Variable Dictionary

  • species: Penguin species: Adelie, Chinstrap, or Gentoo
  • island: Island where the penguin was observed: Biscoe, Dream, or Torgersen
  • bill_length_mm: Bill length in millimeters
  • bill_depth_mm: Bill depth in millimeters
  • flipper_length_mm: Flipper length in millimeters
  • body_mass_g: Body mass in grams
  • sex: Penguin sex: female or male
  • year: Study year: 2007, 2008, or 2009

Data Source

Data were collected by Palmer Station Antarctica LTER and Dr. Kristen Gorman.

Gorman KB, Williams TD, and Fraser WR (2014). Ecological Sexual Dimorphism and Environmental Variability within a Community of Antarctic Penguins (Genus Pygoscelis). PLoS ONE, 9(3), e90081.

Repository: Environmental Data Initiative. doi:10.6073/pasta/98b16d7d563f265cb52372c8ca99e60f

Exercise 01: Importing and Cleaning Data

The file penguins.xlsx is an Excel file. R does not read Excel files using its basic built-in functions, so we will use the readxl package.

The code below first loads the tidyverse package. It then checks whether readxl is installed. If necessary, R will install the package and then load it.

  • Run the following code.
library(tidyverse)
## ── Attaching core tidyverse packages ──────────────────────── tidyverse 2.0.0 ──
## ✔ dplyr     1.2.1     ✔ readr     2.2.0
## ✔ forcats   1.0.1     ✔ stringr   1.6.0
## ✔ ggplot2   4.0.3     ✔ tibble    3.3.1
## ✔ lubridate 1.9.5     ✔ tidyr     1.3.2
## ✔ purrr     1.2.2     
## ── Conflicts ────────────────────────────────────────── tidyverse_conflicts() ──
## ✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter()
## ✖ dplyr::lag()    masks stats::lag()
## ℹ Use the conflicted package (<http://conflicted.r-lib.org/>) to force all conflicts to become errors
if (!require(readxl)) {
  install.packages(
    "readxl",
    repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org/"
  )
}
## Loading required package: readxl
library(readxl)

df_penguins <- read_xlsx("penguins.xlsx")
  • Use summary() to obtain a quick overview of the dataset. (5 Points)
summary(df_penguins)
##       species          island    bill_length_mm  bill_depth_mm  
##  Length   :344   Length   :344   Min.   :32.10   Min.   :13.10  
##  N.unique :  3   N.unique :  3   1st Qu.:39.23   1st Qu.:15.60  
##  N.blank  :  0   N.blank  :  0   Median :44.45   Median :17.30  
##  Min.nchar:  6   Min.nchar:  5   Mean   :43.92   Mean   :17.15  
##  Max.nchar:  9   Max.nchar:  9   3rd Qu.:48.50   3rd Qu.:18.70  
##                                  Max.   :59.60   Max.   :21.50  
##                                  NAs    :2       NAs    :2      
##  flipper_length_mm  body_mass_g          sex           year     
##  Min.   :172.0     Min.   :2700   Length   :344   Min.   :2007  
##  1st Qu.:190.0     1st Qu.:3550   N.unique :  2   1st Qu.:2007  
##  Median :197.0     Median :4050   N.blank  :  0   Median :2008  
##  Mean   :200.9     Mean   :4202   Min.nchar:  4   Mean   :2008  
##  3rd Qu.:213.0     3rd Qu.:4750   Max.nchar:  6   3rd Qu.:2009  
##  Max.   :231.0     Max.   :6300   NAs      : 11   Max.   :2009  
##  NAs    :2         NAs    :2

You should notice NA values in several variables, including bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm, flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g, and sex.

NA represents a missing or unavailable value. In a real research project, researchers should carefully investigate why data are missing before removing observations. For this introductory lab, we will simply remove observations containing missing values.

The symbol |> is called the pipe operator. It sends the object on the left side of the operator into the function on the right side. In the code below, the dataset df_penguins is passed to drop_na(), which removes rows containing missing values.

  • Run the following code to create a cleaned dataset.
df_penguins_clean <- df_penguins |>
  drop_na()
  • Now summarize the cleaned dataset. (5 Points)
summary(df_penguins_clean)
##       species          island    bill_length_mm  bill_depth_mm  
##  Length   :333   Length   :333   Min.   :32.10   Min.   :13.10  
##  N.unique :  3   N.unique :  3   1st Qu.:39.50   1st Qu.:15.60

##  Min.nchar:  6   Min.nchar:  5   Mean   :43.99   Mean   :17.16  
##  Max.nchar:  9   Max.nchar:  9   3rd Qu.:48.60   3rd Qu.:18.70  
##                                  Max.   :59.60   Max.   :21.50  
##  flipper_length_mm  body_mass_g          sex           year     
##  Min.   :172       Min.   :2700   Length   :333   Min.   :2007  
##  1st Qu.:190       1st Qu.:3550   N.unique :  2   1st Qu.:2007  
##  Median :197       Median :4050   N.blank  :  0   Median :2008  
##  Mean   :201       Mean   :4207   Min.nchar:  4   Mean   :2008  
##  3rd Qu.:213       3rd Qu.:4775   Max.nchar:  6   3rd Qu.:2009  
##  Max.   :231       Max.   :6300                   Max.   :2009
  • Verify that the cleaned dataset no longer contains missing values.

Exercise 02: Median Body Mass by Species

We will now investigate the median body mass for each penguin species.

  • The following code filters the cleaned dataset to include only Adelie penguins and then calculates the median body mass.
df_Adelie_clean <- df_penguins_clean |>
  filter(species == "Adelie")

median(df_Adelie_clean$body_mass_g)
## [1] 3700
  • Use the same approach to calculate the median body mass for Gentoo and Chinstrap penguins. (10 Points)
df_Gentoo_clean <- df_penguins_clean |>
  filter(species == "Gentoo")

df_Chinstrap_clean <- df_penguins_clean |>
  filter(species == "Chinstrap")

median(df_Gentoo_clean$body_mass_g)
## [1] 5050
median(df_Chinstrap_clean$body_mass_g)
## [1] 3700
  • There is also a more efficient way to calculate the median body mass for all species at once. The functions group_by() and summarise() allow us to group observations and calculate summary statistics for each group. Review help(group_by) and help(summarise). (Bonus: 10 Points)
df_penguins_clean |>
  group_by(species) |>
  summarise(median_mass = median(body_mass_g))
## # A tibble: 3 × 2
##   species   median_mass
##   <chr>           <dbl>
## 1 Adelie           3700
## 2 Chinstrap        3700
## 3 Gentoo           5050

Exercise 03: Boxplot for Adelie Penguins

  • Create a horizontal boxplot showing the distribution of body mass for Adelie penguins.

Your figure should include:

  • the correct dataset; (5 points)
  • a boxplot; (5 points)
  • an informative x-axis label; an informative y-axis label; a descriptive title; and (5 points)
  • a fill color of your choice. (5 points)
ggplot(
  data = df_Adelie_clean,
  aes(x = body_mass_g, y = species)
) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "steelblue", color = "black") +
  labs(
    x = "Body Mass (g)",
    y = "Species",
    title = "Body Mass Distribution for Adelie Penguins"
  )

Exercise 04: Histogram for Adelie Penguins

Create a histogram showing the distribution of body mass for Adelie penguins. Choose a reasonable bin width so that the overall shape of the distribution is visible without creating too many or too few bars. Your figure should include:

  • the correct dataset; (5 points)
  • a histogram; (5 points)
  • an informative x-axis label; an informative y-axis label; * a descriptive title; and (5 points)
  • a reasonable bin width (binwidth = 80 or other vlaues you find reasonable). (5 points)
ggplot(
  data = df_Adelie_clean,
  aes(x = body_mass_g)
) +
  geom_histogram(
    binwidth = 80,
    fill = "steelblue",
    color = "black"
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Body Mass (g)",
    y = "Number of Penguins",
    title = "Distribution of Body Mass for Adelie Penguins"
  )

Exercise 05: Frequency Table and Bar Chart

  • First, use table() to count the number of observations for each penguin species. Use the format dataframe$variable_name to extract the species variable. (5 Points)
table(df_penguins_clean$species)
## 
##    Adelie Chinstrap    Gentoo 
##       146        68       119
  • Next, create a bar chart showing the number of penguins in each species.

Your bar chart should include:

  • the correct species counts; (5 points)
  • informative axis labels; a descriptive title; (5 points)
  • colors of your choice. (5 points)
ggplot(
  data = df_penguins_clean,
  aes(x = species)
) +
  geom_bar(fill = "steelblue", color = "black") +
  labs(
    x = "Species",
    y = "Number of Penguins",
    title = "Number of Penguins by Species"
  )

Compare the frequency table and the bar chart. Do the counts shown in the table agree with the heights of the bars?

Exercise 06: Comparing Species

  • Create a boxplot showing body mass for all three penguin species. Use the cleaned dataset. You should include informative axis labels and a descriptive title. (5 Points)
ggplot(
  data = df_penguins_clean,
  aes(x = body_mass_g, y = species)
) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    x = "Body Mass (g)",
    y = "Species",
    title = "Body Mass Distribution by Penguin Species"
  )

  • Which penguin specie has the highest median? (5 Points)

  • Next, create a scatterplot showing the relationship between bill length and bill depth for Chinstrap penguins. Again, please provide meaningful labels and figure title. (5 Points)

ggplot(
  data = df_Chinstrap_clean,
  aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm)
) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    x = "Bill Length (mm)",
    y = "Bill Depth (mm)",
    title = "Bill Length and Bill Depth for Chinstrap Penguins"
  )

  • Do you think there is an association between bill length and bill depth for Chinstrap penguins? If so, how would you describe or quantify the relationship? (5 Points)

  • Finally, create scatterplots showing the relationship between bill length and bill depth for all three species. Use facet_wrap() to create a separate panel for each species. Use help(facet_wrap) to read the manual. (Bonus: 10 Points)

ggplot(
  data = df_penguins_clean,
  aes(x = bill_length_mm, y = bill_depth_mm)
) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(vars(species), ncol = 3) +
  labs(
    x = "Bill Length (mm)",
    y = "Bill Depth (mm)",
    title = "Bill Length and Bill Depth by Penguin Species"
  )
